title: God Drew a Line Through This Family: Why Scripture Forbade a Man From Taking Both a Woman and Her Mother
paragraphs: God Drew a Line Through This Family: Why Scripture Forbade a Man From Taking Both a Woman and Her Mother

There is something disturbing buried inside Israel’s sexual laws—and when you understand why God called it זִמָּה, “depravity,” you begin to see that this ancient command was never merely about an ancient household. It exposes what happens whenever human desire decides that another person's sacred boundaries no longer matter.
There are verses in the Bible people hurry past.
Not because they are boring.
Because they are uncomfortable.
Leviticus 18:17 is one of them.
And before we go any further, we need to correct something that is often repeated incorrectly.
The prohibition we are examining is not actually stated in Deuteronomy as the command forbidding a man from taking both a woman and her mother.
The explicit prohibition appears in Leviticus.
That matters.
Because if we are going to defend Scripture, preach Scripture, share Scripture, or build our lives upon Scripture, we must love God's Word enough to let it correct even our headlines.
The Hebrew text says:
“עֶרְוַת אִשָּׁה וּבִתָּהּ לֹא תְגַלֵּה ... שַׁאֲרָה הֵנָּה זִמָּה הִוא”
‘Ervat ishah u-vittah lo tegalleh ... she'erah hennah, zimmah hi.

In context, the command forbids uncovering the nakedness of a woman and her daughter and extends the boundary to close descendants. They are near kin. The text concludes with two chilling Hebrew words:
זִמָּה הִוא — zimmah hi.
“It is depravity.”
That final word matters.
Zimmah.
Not romance.
Not merely an unconventional family arrangement.
Not desire that somehow became inconvenient.
God names what human appetite would rather rename.
And that may be where this ancient passage suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because sin has always been talented at changing vocabulary.
What God calls greed, we can call ambition.
What God calls pride, we can call self-confidence.
What God calls lust, we can call chemistry.
What God calls adultery, a culture can call following your heart.
What God calls darkness, the human heart keeps searching for softer words to describe.
But Scripture refuses to flatter us into destruction.
Sometimes grace begins when God finally calls something what it really is.

Leviticus 18 places boundaries around sexual relationships inside the family and community. The prohibition concerning a woman and her daughter belongs to that larger collection of boundaries. Later, Leviticus 20:14 addresses the specific case of a man taking a woman and her mother and again uses the word zimmah.
That repetition is significant.
This was not merely about two women competing for one man's affection.
Something deeper was being violated.
Kinship itself was being violated.
The family was not supposed to become a hunting ground for appetite.
Think about the emotional reality behind the command.
A woman should not have to wonder whether the man joined to her is secretly looking at her daughter.
A daughter should not become her mother's sexual rival.
A mother should not become her daughter's rival.
Family affection should not be poisoned by predatory comparison.
The household should not become a place where everybody wonders who will become the next object of someone's desire.
God drew a boundary.
And boundaries are not always evidence that God wants to deprive human beings.
Sometimes boundaries are evidence that God sees exactly what human beings can do to one another when desire becomes sovereign.
That distinction matters.
Because our age frequently treats desire as though desire itself creates moral permission.
“I want this.”
“I feel this.”
“This makes me happy.”
“This feels authentic.”
And somewhere along the way, desire quietly moves from witness to judge.
But the Bible repeatedly asks a harder question.
Not merely, “What do I want?”
But:
“What does God call holy?”
That question reaches far beyond ancient Israel.
It reaches into bedrooms.
Phones.
Private messages.
Secret browser histories.
Workplace flirtations.
Emotional affairs.
Pornography.
Hidden relationships.
Relationships we know require somebody else's devastation before they can become ours.
It reaches the place where almost every serious temptation eventually takes us:
“I know where the boundary is...
but I want what is on the other side.”
That is why this strange Old Testament command can suddenly become a mirror.
Maybe you have never desired a woman and her mother.
Maybe the literal scenario feels impossibly distant from your life.
But perhaps you know what it means to negotiate with a boundary.
Perhaps you know what it is to keep a conversation alive because you enjoy being wanted.
Perhaps you deleted messages because you knew what they would look like in daylight.
Perhaps you kept telling yourself, “Nothing has happened.”
Yet.
Perhaps you have watched pornography while convincing everyone around you that your spiritual life was healthy.
Perhaps you have crossed boundaries nobody knows about.
Perhaps you became emotionally attached to somebody else's spouse.
Perhaps you are the spouse who discovered it.
Perhaps you were the child who watched adult desire rip a household apart.
Perhaps you are carrying shame from something you did years ago and still believe that if Christians knew the whole story, they would never look at you the same way again.
Now the passage is no longer ancient.
Now it has your heartbeat.
Because the deepest issue was never merely that one particular arrangement was prohibited.
The deeper issue is what happens when desire refuses to kneel.
Sin whispers:
Take.
God says:
Trust Me.
Sin says:
You deserve this.
God says:
Do not destroy what I have called you to protect.
Sin says:
Nobody will know.
God says:
I already do.
And perhaps that sentence hurts.
Because He knows.
The messages.
The fantasies.
The betrayal.
The affair.
The secret relationship.
The compromise.
The years you wasted.
The people you wounded.
The things you watched.
The person you used.
The marriage you damaged.
The promise you broke.
The version of yourself you desperately hope nobody ever discovers.
He knows.
And now we arrive at the moment where Christianity becomes either unbearably terrifying...
or unimaginably beautiful.
Because the God who knows is also the God who came looking for sinners.
The Bible does not end at Leviticus.
The story keeps moving.
Through sacrifice.
Through covenant.
Through failure.
Through prophets crying for repentance.
Through kings who fell.
Through adulterers.
Liars.
Cowards.
Religious hypocrites.
Broken families.
Scandal after scandal after scandal.
Until eventually...
Jesus Christ walks into the story.
And suddenly holiness has a face.
The One who never crossed God's boundaries walked among people who had shattered them.
He did not redefine sin to make sinners comfortable.
And He did not refuse sinners because their history was filthy.
That combination is the breathtaking scandal of grace.
Jesus could say, in effect:
What you did was sin.
And still say:
Come to Me.
The Gospel does not rescue us by pretending darkness is light.
Jesus rescues us by entering our darkness and bringing us into His light.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace finally makes us brave enough to stop running.
The New Testament word often associated with repentance is the Greek μετάνοια — metanoia.
It speaks of a profound turning—a changed mind and orientation that bears fruit in a changed life.
Not:
“I am sorry I got caught.”
Not:
“I will hide it better.”
Not:
“Everybody makes mistakes.”
But:
“Jesus, I was wrong.
You were right.
Have mercy on me.
Change me.”
And Christ receives repentant sinners.
That is not sentimental Christianity.
That is Christianity.
At the cross, Jesus does something astonishing with scandal.
He does not excuse it.
He bears sin's judgment.
He does not announce that holiness no longer matters.
He demonstrates how much it matters.
He does not tell humanity that rebellion was harmless.
The cross tells us precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption cost blood.
And God's love is so staggering that Christ willingly gave His.
This is why the Gospel is more powerful than shame.
Shame says:
“Hide.”
Jesus says:
“Come.”
Shame says:
“You are only what you did.”
Jesus offers a new identity to those who belong to Him.
Shame says:
“Your story is finished.”
The risen Christ says otherwise.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not because scandal becomes acceptable.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes the sexually broken and teaches purity.
He takes adulterers and teaches faithfulness.
He takes liars and teaches truth.
He takes the proud and teaches surrender.
He takes the ashamed and clothes them with grace.
He takes people who thought their secret would be the final chapter...
and begins writing something new.
Maybe this article found you while you are still hiding.
Then stop reading for a moment.
Not because God is finished with you.
Because maybe you are finally ready to stop pretending.
You do not need better camouflage.
You need Christ.
You do not need to become skilled at appearing holy.
You need the Holy One.
You do not need another promise whispered to yourself at 2:00 in the morning that you will “never do it again.”
You need repentance.
Grace.
Accountability.
Truth.
The Spirit of God.
And the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Bring Him what you have been hiding.
Confess your sin to God.
Turn from what you know is evil.
Where appropriate and safe, seek wise Christian accountability and make righteous amends for harm you have caused.
Do not use “grace” as permission to remain inside the thing Christ is calling you out of.
Grace is not Jesus helping you decorate your prison.
Grace opens the door.
Walk out.
And if this exposed something hidden inside you, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail.
But you can stop pretending.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer fighting a battle behind a smile.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally confess their own struggle because you were courageous enough to admit that you need Christ too.
Not to expose them.
Not to embarrass them.
Send it because sometimes love says:
Please don't disappear into the darkness. Jesus is still calling you home.
Because biblical truth should not merely be consumed.
It should transform us.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases salvation. It cannot.
Jesus Christ alone saves.

But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical, voluntary way of helping Scripture-centered teaching reach more people. If you genuinely believe this ministry glorifies Christ and serves His people, consider supporting it—not from guilt or spiritual pressure, but freely, prayerfully, and joyfully.
Not because sharing an article proves your faith.
Not because an algorithm glorifies God.
But because somewhere in your circle may be a person who will never walk into a church this week...
One share can become somebody else's midnight reading.
One tag can reach the friend who stopped talking about their struggle.
One saved article can return to you during temptation.
One honest comment can give another wounded believer permission to stop hiding.
That must always remain the point.
Because Moses can show us the boundary.
The Law can expose the transgression.
The Hebrew word zimmah can force us to stop giving beautiful names to destructive things.
But only Jesus can save the sinner.
Only Jesus can forgive.
Only Jesus can cleanse.
Only Jesus can take the person whispering, “If everyone knew what I had done, my story would be over,” and write a chapter that shame never imagined.
So when the enemy drags your old scandal back into the courtroom of your mind, remember this:
Your worst chapter does not get the authority to write your final sentence when your life has been surrendered to Jesus Christ.
